title: MIT Researchers Develop New Method to Accelerate Search for Green Ammonia Catalysts
excerpt: A computational approach could help identify materials that make electrochemical ammonia production viable, potentially reducing the industry's 1.5% share of global greenhouse emissions.
body:
• MIT researchers developed a computational method to predict which materials could serve as effective catalysts for electrochemical ammonia production, bypassing years of trial-and-error testing
  • Ammonia production accounts for roughly 2% of global energy consumption and 1.5% of greenhouse gas emissions, nearly all through the century-old Haber-Bosch process
  • The study, published in the Royal Society of Chemistry journal EES Catalysis, focused on transition metal nitride compounds as promising catalyst candidates
  • The approach is still theoretical — identified alloys must be synthesized and tested in laboratory reaction cells before any industrial application

Researchers at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology have developed a computational method that could significantly accelerate the search for catalysts capable of making green ammonia production economically viable, according to a study published this week in the journal EES Catalysis.

Ammonia, the world's second most-produced chemical after sulfuric acid, is essential for fertilizer manufacturing that sustains global food production. But the dominant production method — the Haber-Bosch process, in use for more than a century — relies on fossil fuels to generate extreme heat and pressure, consuming roughly 2% of the world's energy and producing about 1.5% of global greenhouse gas emissions.

From Trial and Error to Targeted Discovery

An alternative electrochemical approach exists that uses electricity rather than fossil fuels, but it has never achieved the efficiency needed for industrial-scale production. The bottleneck lies in finding the right catalyst — a material that can drive the necessary chemical reactions efficiently enough to compete on cost.

"Our approach identifies the key physical properties that drive catalytic activity in ammonia production."

— Bilge Yildiz, Breen M. Kerr Professor, MIT

Rather than testing millions of possible alloy combinations through laboratory experiments — a process that can take years — the MIT team used density functional theory, a quantum mechanics-based computational method, to simulate how different atomic arrangements would perform as catalysts. They then combined these simulations with machine learning to identify which physical properties most influence catalytic activity.

The researchers focused on transition metal nitrides, a class of compounds that have shown particular promise because the nitrogen within the catalyst itself participates in the reaction. This creates a chain of chemical steps where each stage partially powers the next, reducing the total energy input required.

Key Bottlenecks Identified

The study pinpointed specific bottlenecks in the nitrogen reduction reaction pathway, including nitrogen dissociation and hydrogen transfer, that limit current catalyst performance. By understanding which material properties govern these steps, the researchers can now narrow the field of candidate alloys rather than searching blindly.

"If we can somehow find a catalyst that reduces the energy needed and is more selective for ammonia production, then we could essentially hit the jackpot," said Constantine Athanitis, a doctoral student in MIT's Department of Materials Science and Engineering and a co-author of the paper.

The world currently uses about 200 million metric tons of ammonia annually, and demand is expected to grow as populations increase. Beyond fertilizer, ammonia is also gaining attention as a potential hydrogen carrier for clean energy transport.

A Long Road to Application

Dane Morgan, a professor of engineering at the University of Wisconsin who was not involved in the study, described the work as "exciting" and said it could help build a foundation for designing new catalysts. However, he cautioned that "translating these calculations into practical catalysts will require many additional steps, so meaningful real-world impact is likely still some distance away."

The next phase will involve building laboratory reaction cells to test the most promising alloys under real operating conditions. The researchers acknowledge this transition from theory to practice remains the critical challenge.

"For this to really make an impact in society, we need to bring it to the experimental lab," Athanitis said. "We like to think we've pushed the boundary of candidate materials beyond what was thought of before."
